title: Ending with dignity
hook: a divorce document, and a hope for kindness on both sides

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was shalom bayit, and your line was peace at home. What small peace did you make? Today, the hard case: when a home cannot hold its peace any longer. Day one thousand three hundred twelve.

A scribe dips a quill. Around the table sit a rabbinic court of three and two witnesses, and across from them, two people who once stood under a canopy together. The scribe writes a short document by hand, on purpose, for this one couple, with their names spelled out with care. It is folded. Then it is placed into her hands, and she takes it. That is all. No shouting, no verdict about who was right. Jewish law knows that some marriages end. The question it keeps asking is how. Today is about that how: ending with dignity.
screen: `A COURT OF THREE.` → `A DOCUMENT WRITTEN BY HAND.` → `PLACED INTO HER HANDS.`

segments.voice: The document is called a get. Its root is in the Torah itself. In Deuteronomy, the old Jewish Publication Society translation describes a husband who "writeth her a bill of divorcement, and giveth it in her hand." Turn that line four ways. First, it is written. A divorce in Jewish law is not a mood or a slammed door. It is a careful act, done in front of witnesses, so that no one is left wondering whether they are free. Clarity is its own kind of kindness. Second, it is given into a hand. The ending happens person to person. In traditional law the husband gives and the wife receives, and both must do it willingly. Third, the sorrow is allowed. The prophet Malachi has God say, "For I hate putting away." And the Talmud adds a picture that some readers never forget: when a man divorces the wife of his youth, even the altar sheds tears. Divorce is permitted, and it is still a loss worth grieving. Fourth, the hard part, said plainly. Because the get must be given freely, a spouse can refuse to give it, and a woman can be left unable to remarry. She is called an agunah, a chained woman. Rabbis and communities have worked on this for a long time, and today some couples sign agreements before the wedding so that no one is ever trapped. That is the hope underneath it all: kindness on both sides, even at the end. A marriage that began with blessings can close with honesty, clear words, and no one humiliated.
screen: `IT IS WRITTEN.` · `GIVEN INTO A HAND.` · `EVEN THE ALTAR SHEDS TEARS.` · `NO ONE LEFT CHAINED.` · then, large: `END WITH DIGNITY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: end one thing kindly. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something in your life that is ending, or should. A job, a project, a habit, a friendship that has run its course, a group chat you've quietly left. Don't fix it now. Just ask three questions, one per few breaths. Is the ending clear, so no one is left guessing? Is it person to person, not a vanishing act? Is there anything kind I could still say? Let one honest, gentle sentence form. If you pray, you can hold the people on the other side of that ending in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Ending with dignity. A get written by hand, given into a hand, a loss allowed to be a loss, and no one left chained. Today's word.

Your line: end with dignity. Today, close one small thing properly: reply to the message you've been avoiding, say goodbye instead of fading out, or thank someone on your way out the door. Day one thousand three hundred twelve.

howItsDone: In traditional Jewish law a marriage ends with a get, a divorce document written by a scribe and given by the husband to the wife before a rabbinic court and witnesses; some couples today also sign a prenuptial agreement meant to ensure a get is never withheld.

trapdoor: what you thought: a Jewish divorce is just a court ruling.
what it means: a get, written by hand and given into a hand, so the ending is clear and done willingly.
what a scholar hears: Deuteronomy 24, Malachi 2, Gittin 90b's weeping altar, and the long work to free the agunah.

sources.quoted: writeth her a bill of divorcement, and giveth it in her hand

sources.ref: Mishnah Gittin; Yevamot 112b (consent of both parties, later codified)

notes: Deuteronomy 24:1 and Malachi 2:16 quoted from JPS 1917; confirm exact wording.
Gittin 90b (the altar sheds tears over one who divorces his first wife) paraphrased; confirm.
Hook describes a beit din of three, a scribe, two witnesses; confirm this is a fair general description across communities.

'Both must do it willingly' reflects the later rule (attributed to Rabbeinu Gershom) that a wife cannot be divorced against her will, alongside the requirement that the husband give freely; Keeper to confirm the phrasing and source line (Yevamot 112b is approximate).
Agunah and prenuptial agreements: kept general ('some couples'); confirm fair across Orthodox and liberal communities. Reform practice differs on requiring a get; Keeper may want a line.
Outline word is the title head 'Ending with dignity'; original game uses get.
Editor: hook opener changed from 'A small room' to the scribe's quill, so it no longer echoes day 1309's 'A small side room' opening.
